results.summary_before: Zinnia+ is a minimal 8-bit CPU based on the Harvard architecture, with internal data memory and external program memory accessed through the I/O pins. It uses a 6-bit instruction length and multiplexes the output between the program counter and the accumulator. The design requires external program memory and a bus demultiplexer for operation. It is notable for its extreme simplicity and educational value, with a testbench provided to compute prime numbers.

results.summary_before: This design computes the square root of a 7-bit integer in 4.2 fixed-point format, rounding down to the nearest quarter. It uses Newton's method and produces a result after three clock cycles. The inputs are the 7-bit value and a clock, and the output is a 6-bit fixed-point number. Optionally, a binary-to-BCD converter can be added to display the result, but no other external hardware is required.

results.summary_before: tiny egg timer is a configurable countdown timer implemented as a three-state finite state machine (Idle, Waiting, Alarm) with counters for clock cycles, seconds and minutes. The user sets a wait time in minutes on five input pins and asserts start; a 7-segment display shows the countdown with the decimal point toggling each second, and an 'A' is displayed when the time expires. The alarm is stopped by deasserting the start switch, and no external hardware is required. The documentation is brief but sufficient to describe the intended operation and test procedure.

results.summary_before: This design is an I2C peripheral that implements an 8-bit ALU to perform pattern testing and accumulate results, functioning as a bit error rate tester (BERT). It connects to an I2C controller (such as an RP2040) via the bidirectional pins and can be configured for different clocking modes and bus types through input pins. The design outputs results on a 7-segment display and includes power-on-reset configuration options. The documentation is somewhat technical and notes that further updates are planned, but it provides sufficient detail for operation.

results.summary_before: This is an RV32IMA RISC-V SoC capable of booting and running uLinux, with UART, SPI, and LED interfaces. It requires flashing a bootloader, device tree, and Linux image onto an external NOR flash, and a 22 pF capacitor on the NOR flash clock line was needed for reliable operation. Silicon tests by the author and testers confirmed successful Linux boot at around 30.5 MHz. The design includes a divider register for configuring the CLINT and UART.
